drapeaux.note: « the many charms and magical potions without which no native believes he could live » : citation de Horace Miner (original en anglais, Body Ritual among the Nacirema, 1956), retraduite depuis le français ; à comparer à l'original.
« guérisseurs » rendu par « medicine men » (terme de la fiche en quiz) et « hommes à la bouche sainte » par « holy-mouth men » ; à vérifier contre le texte de Miner.

accroche: “Nacirema” is just “American” read backward, and the ritual described is tooth brushing.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1956, the journal American Anthropologist publishes an ethnographic study of a North American people, the Nacirema. The text describes their beliefs with the detachment usually reserved for the most exotic peoples: a people obsessed with the body, convinced that it is naturally prone to illness and ugliness, and which devotes to daily rituals an energy that few societies expend on their religion. The people's name, read backward, gives the key to the article: Nacirema is American.

## The shrine, the medicine man, and the mouth rite

The author, the anthropologist Horace Miner, describes what a reader quickly recognizes as his own bathroom under the name “shrine”: every Nacirema household is said to have at least one, built around a wall cabinet where are kept “the many charms and magical potions without which no native believes he could live.” The most powerful of the practitioners, the “medicine men,” do not prepare these potions themselves: they merely prescribe the ingredients, in exchange for generous gifts. A separate caste, the “holy-mouth men,” practices every day a rite that Miner, as a foreign observer, finds downright repugnant: inserting a bundle of hog hairs into the mouth and rubbing the gums according to a painstaking ritual. It takes the reader a few paragraphs to recognize toothpaste and the toothbrush.

## Making strange what we no longer see

The article is not a one-off joke. It is a demonstration of method. By applying to his own society the detached vocabulary an ethnographer usually reserves for distant cultures, Miner shows that exoticism is not a property of the people observed. It is an effect of the gaze we turn on them. A ritual seems strange only when we stop already knowing what it means. The most banal gesture, brushing your teeth, becomes visible again, almost incomprehensible, as soon as you describe it without the word that makes it familiar.

A former president of the Society for Applied Anthropology, Miner teaches by this detour what ethnography requires in any field, including one's own: suspending what you think you already know. The article has since been reprinted in more than fifty collections and academic anthologies in a little over five decades, according to a study that traced its history in 2014. It is one of the most republished social-science texts of the 20th century in English, cited whenever the point is to learn to look at your own culture as if you did not come from it.

repere.texte: Published in 1956, Miner's article has since been reprinted in more than fifty collections and academic anthologies in a little over five decades, one of the most republished English-language social-science texts of the 20th century.
repere.source: Mark Burde, “Social-Science Fiction: The Genesis and Legacy of Horace Miner's "Body Ritual among the Nacirema"”, American Anthropologist, vol. 116, no. 3, 2014, pp. 549-561

carte.idee: In 1956, Horace Miner describes the bodily rituals of a fictional North American people, the Nacirema, with the detached vocabulary of an ethnographer facing an exotic culture. It takes the reader a few paragraphs to recognize their own tooth brushing in the “holy-mouth rite.”

quiz.question: Why does Horace Miner describe tooth brushing as an exotic ritual rather than as a simple hygiene routine?
choix: Because the Nacirema did not actually use toothpaste
Because the journal American Anthropologist required religious vocabulary
To reveal the arbitrariness of a familiar gesture, once you do not know what it means
To prove that Western societies practiced a form of sorcery
quiz.explication: It is a demonstration of method: describing your own society with the detached vocabulary of ethnography shows that exoticism lies in the gaze turned on a gesture, not in the gesture itself. Neither the product used, nor a journal's instruction, nor an accusation of sorcery explains the approach.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do the “medicine men” described by Miner do, according to the text of the card?
choix: They prepare the potions themselves and distribute them free to the sick
They prescribe the ingredients of the potions, in exchange for generous gifts, without preparing them themselves
They perform the daily holy-mouth rite in place of their patients
They live as recluses in the shrine and never see patients
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that the medicine men do not prepare the potions themselves: they merely prescribe the ingredients, in return for generous gifts.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is the “shrine” that Miner describes in every Nacirema household?
choix: A communal temple reserved for the village's collective ceremonies
A room where only ritual food is stored
A family burial place located under each house
A wall cabinet where charms and magical potions are kept, in every household
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Miner describes a wall cabinet present in every Nacirema household, where are kept the charms and magical potions without which, he says, no native believes he could live.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What position had Horace Miner held before the publication of his article, according to the card?
choix: He had been president of the Society for Applied Anthropology
He headed the anthropology department at Harvard University
He was editor-in-chief of the journal American Anthropologist
He had just received the Nobel Prize in Literature for his ethnographic work
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The card specifies that Miner, a former president of the Society for Applied Anthropology, applies to his own culture the detached gaze he teaches elsewhere.
